c.tagline: Turquoise water, colonial streets, island time.

taxi.fareNote: Taxi fares in New Providence are set by government zone-based rate cards rather than meters; agree on/confirm the fare before departure.

emergency.note: 919 is the traditional national emergency line; 911 also connects to police/ambulance/fire in New Providence. Princess Margaret Hospital is the main public hospital.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Caution "Over the Hill" (south of Bay St); tourist areas (Cable Beach, Paradise Island) safe

hood_desc: A mega-resort strip anchored by Baha Mar with a long public beach, casinos, golf and nightlife; suits resort-and-relax travelers and couples wanting all-inclusive convenience.
Home to the iconic Atlantis mega-resort, marina, Aquaventure water park and Comfort Suites; suits families, cruisers with a stopover night, and anyone who wants beach plus theme-park energy.

The historic colonial core with Bay Street shopping, Government House, museums, the Straw Market and cruise port; suits history buffs, first-timers, and travelers without a car who want to walk everywhere.

A quieter residential/marina area with a long public beach (Saunders Beach) and canal-front condos a short drive from downtown; suits longer stays, families, and budget-to-midrange travelers wanting local flavor.
Leafy, low-key upscale residential stretch near Fort Montagu and Montagu Bay with small inns and guesthouses; suits travelers wanting a quieter, more local, less touristy base close to downtown.
lodging: British Colonial Nassau, Curio Collection by Hilton

water.note: Tap water meets safety standards, though it can taste of chlorine or salt; bottled water is common by preference.

transit.pay: Jitney buses are cash-only, pay the driver directly in exact or near-exact Bahamian/US dollars as you board (flat fare regardless of distance). The Paradise Island ferry and water taxis are also paid in cash at the dock or on board.
transit.hours: Jitneys run roughly 6:30am-10pm on most routes with no true late-night service; taxis operate 24 hours.
transit.note: There is no rail or formal metro; privately-operated numbered jitney buses cover New Providence and are the main low-cost public transport, supplemented by taxis, water taxis to Paradise Island, and rental cars/scooters.

bus: Nassau Jitney public bus network (numbered routes across New Providence)
ferry: Bahamas Ferries (inter-island service from Potter's Cay)

transit.m: Taxi (fixed zone fare to Cable Beach/Downtown)
Jitney bus #10 or #32 to downtown (~40-50 min)

tip.r: 15% is standard at restaurants (many add an automatic gratuity for larger groups); tip hotel porters $1-2/bag and housekeeping a few dollars/day; tour guides and taxi drivers 10-15%.

food.name: Conch salad
food.desc: Raw conch diced at the stall with onion, sweet pepper and tomato, then cured in lime and sour orange juice. The Bahamian national snack, eaten with a fork.

places.name: Potter's Cay Dock stalls
places.note: Working conch shacks under the Paradise Island bridge; the conch is cracked in front of you.

places.name: Goldie's Conch House
places.note: Fish Fry stalwart in pastel paint; conch salad plus the coldest Kalik on the strip.

places.name: Twin Brothers
places.note: One of the busiest Fish Fry restaurants, known for conch in every form.

food.name: Cracked conch
food.desc: Conch pounded tender, battered and deep-fried golden, served with peas and rice, plantain and a hot lime-pepper sauce.

places.name: Twin Brothers
places.note: Fish Fry favourite for cracked conch and conch fritters; loud, local and busy.

places.name: The Poop Deck
places.note: Serving Bahamian seafood since 1972 with harbour views; conch chowder is excellent too.

places.name: Goldie's Conch House
places.note: Long-running Fish Fry kitchen where locals eat as much as visitors.

food.name: Bahamian rock lobster
food.desc: Clawless spiny lobster from Bahamian waters, split and grilled or served as a creamy lobster salad. Season runs August to March.

places.name: The Poop Deck
places.note: Grilled crawfish tail done simply, with harbour views and a long rum list.

places.name: Graycliff Restaurant
places.note: Colonial mansion with a vast wine cellar; the formal end of Bahamian dining.

places.name: Lukka Kairi
places.note: Waterfront restaurant on the downtown strip with live music and Bahamian seafood.

food.name: Johnnycake
food.desc: A dense, slightly sweet pan bread baked in a skillet and served in wedges beside conch chowder, stew fish or peas and rice.

places.name: Bahamian Cookin' Restaurant
places.note: Home-style Bahamian cooking a block from Bay Street; a good first local meal.

places.name: Travellers Rest
places.note: Beachside institution west of town; johnnycake with stew fish under the sea grape trees.

places.name: The Shoal Restaurant and Lounge
places.note: Local favourite for okra soup, conch chowder and mutton with peas and rice.

food.name: Stew fish and grits
food.desc: The classic Bahamian breakfast: grouper or snapper stewed in a dark browned-flour gravy or boiled with lime and pepper, served over grits with johnnycake.

places.name: Cricket Club
places.note: Time-capsule colonial balcony overlooking a cricket pitch; tuna and grits, stewed conch, souse.

places.name: Nesbitt's
places.note: More than 40 years of corned beef and grits and boiled grouper for early risers.

places.name: Travellers Rest
places.note: Reliable for souse, boiled fish and stewed conch away from the cruise crowds.

food.name: Guava duff
food.desc: The national dessert: guava-filled dough steamed in a roll, sliced like a pinwheel and flooded with hot butter-rum sauce at the table.

places.name: Bahamian Cookin' Restaurant
places.note: Traditional guava duff with proper rum sauce; order it when you sit down.

places.name: Arawak Cay Fish Fry
places.note: Several stalls sell it by the slice, especially busy on weekend evenings.

places.name: Goldie's Conch House
places.note: Finish a conch lunch here with duff and a Sky Juice.

food.name: Sky Juice
food.desc: Gin, coconut water and sweetened condensed milk with fresh nutmeg grated over the top. Also called gully wash, and dangerously easy to drink.

places.name: Sky Juice King
places.note: Fish Fry stall dedicated to the drink; the straightforward place to try your first.

places.name: Goldie's Conch House
places.note: Often credited as the birthplace of Sky Juice, back in the Prohibition era.

places.name: Bahamian Cookin' Restaurant
places.note: Handy downtown option if you are not heading out to the Fish Fry.

food.name: Kalik beer
food.desc: The Beer of the Bahamas, a light lager named after the clank of Junkanoo cowbells. Ask for Kalik Gold if you want something stronger.

places.name: Arawak Cay Fish Fry
places.note: Every stall and bar pours it ice cold; the natural pairing with conch.

places.name: Lukka Kairi
places.note: Harbourfront bar downtown with live Bahamian music most evenings.

places.name: The Poop Deck
places.note: Sunset Kalik on the deck over Nassau Harbour.

landmarks: Queen's Staircase
Carved by hand out of solid limestone by enslaved workers in the 18th century, these 65 steps flanked by towering cliffs are among Nassau's most striking sights.
Fort Fincastle
This unusual paddle-steamer-shaped 18th-century fort sits atop Bennet's Hill, rewarding visitors with sweeping views over Nassau harbor.
Atlantis Paradise Island Resort
This colossal, pink-towered mega-resort with its bridge-suite and waterpark is the single most recognizable image of Nassau and the Bahamas at large.
Nassau Lighthouse (Hog Island Lighthouse)
One of the oldest surviving lighthouses in the Caribbean, this candy-cane-esque tower on Paradise Island has guided ships since 1817.
Straw Market
A bustling downtown institution since the 1940s, this market is packed with handwoven straw goods and local crafts, capturing authentic Bahamian culture.
Government House, Nassau
This grand pink colonial mansion atop a hill, guarded by a statue of Christopher Columbus, is the official residence of the Bahamas' Governor-General.
Fort Charlotte
The largest fort in the Bahamas, this 18th-century stronghold features a moat, dungeons, and cannons overlooking the harbor.
Rawson Square
The pastel-pink Parliament buildings and a statue of Queen Victoria frame this historic civic square at the heart of downtown Nassau.
Cable Beach
A postcard-perfect stretch of white sand and turquoise water lined with resorts, Cable Beach epitomizes Nassau's tropical appeal.
Prince George Wharf
Nassau's iconic cruise port, lined with colorful straw vendors and a constant parade of towering ships against a bright Caribbean backdrop.

train.note: The Bahamas has no railways at all. Get around New Providence by taxi or local jitney bus; reach other islands by ferry or domestic flight.

bus.note: As an island nation there are no international or long-distance coach routes. Within Nassau, transport is by numbered local jitney buses (cash fare) and taxis; travel between islands is by ferry or plane, not bus.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferry sails from Nassau — the Florida ferries (Baleària Caribbean) run from Fort Lauderdale to Bimini and Freeport/Grand Bahama, not Nassau. From Nassau, Bahamas Ferries (bahamasferries.com) runs domestic fast ferries to Out Islands such as Harbour Island/Spanish Wells (Eleuthera), Governor's Harbour, the Exumas and Andros; traditional mailboats also sail from Potter's Cay.

half.name: Exuma Cays (Pig Beach)
half.blurb: Dazzling chain of cays with swimming pigs, iguanas and impossibly clear turquoise sandbanks.

half.name: Blue Lagoon Island
half.blurb: Private island near Nassau known for dolphin encounters, calm beaches and shady palm groves.

half.name: Rose Island
half.blurb: Secluded island just offshore with quiet sandy beaches and gentle waters for snorkeling.

half.name: Harbour Island
half.blurb: Famous for its blush-colored pink-sand beach, pastel cottages and relaxed island charm.
